```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
library(ggplot2)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment  = "#>",
  fig.width  = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.25,
  warning  = FALSE,
  message  = FALSE
)

# The slice-sampling runs shown below take up to two minutes, so their
# diagnostics, run times, and summaries are stored in the package.
# Regenerate them with the `bayesian-computation` section of
# data-raw/generate_vignette_cache.R.
cache_file <- file.path("..", "inst", "extdata",
                        "cache-bayesian-computation.rds")
if (!file.exists(cache_file)) {
  cache_file <- system.file("extdata", "cache-bayesian-computation.rds",
                            package = "multiScaleR")
}
cache <- readRDS(cache_file)
pilot <- cache$pilot
long  <- cache$long
```

# What this vignette covers

`multiScale_bayes()` can compute the same posterior in several ways. The
`method` argument changes how the answer is computed and how long it takes. It
does not change the model, the likelihood, or the priors. A slow, exact method
and a fast, approximate one can still return different numbers, and this
vignette shows how to choose between them and how to tell when a result is
safe to report.

You will check a model before fitting, run a short pilot, read its
diagnostics, compare five computations of one model, check a probability from
a fast approximation, and work through what to do when a fit struggles. Every result shown is stored in the package, so
nothing here needs sampling software. Read
`vignette("v13-bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR")` first for priors and
model fitting.

# Compare the methods

| `method` | What it computes | Uncertainty you get | Optional packages | Use it |
|:---------|:-----------------|:--------------------|:------------------|:-------|
| `"prepare"` | Checks the formulas, data rows, priors, and landscape inputs. Fits nothing | None | None | Before every fit |
| `"sample"` (default) | Draws from the full posterior with NUTS, a gradient-based Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler | Full posterior, with chain diagnostics | RTMB, tmbstan, rstan, posterior | For results you will report |
| `"slice"` | Draws from the same posterior with a slice sampler written in R | Full posterior, with chain diagnostics | None to fit, posterior for diagnostics | When you cannot install the NUTS software, and for small models |
| `"laplace"` | Finds the peak of the posterior and fits one Gaussian curve around it | Approximate. Symmetric on the model's internal log scale | RTMB | To explore while you build a model |
| `"marginal"` | Integrates the spread of one scale among groups numerically, with a Gaussian approximation for everything else | Approximate. The spread among groups can be skewed | RTMB | When sampling is too slow and the model has one such spread |
| `"marginal"` with `control = list(correction = "importance")` | Reweights draws from the marginal approximation against the full posterior | Targets the full posterior, with weight diagnostics | RTMB, posterior | As a check on the marginal approximation |

The *posterior* is the distribution of parameter values supported by the data
and the priors. Sampling methods draw from it directly, in several independent
runs called *chains*. Approximations replace it with a simpler shape that is
fast to compute. The whole interface is experimental, and the importance
correction most of all.

# Check the software and the model

`check_bayes_setup()` reports whether the optional packages for a method are
installed. It installs nothing and fits nothing.

```{r setup-check}
setup <- check_bayes_setup("sample")       # also "slice", "laplace", "marginal"
setup$packages[c("package", "minimum")]    # packages NUTS needs, minimum versions
```

`setup$ready` is `TRUE` when every listed package loads and meets its minimum
version. That says nothing about memory or about how well a model will sample.
Add `cores = 2` to the call to check the `processx` package, which parallel
fits need.

Next, check the model itself. `method = "prepare"` matches each observation to
its landscape inputs, builds the formulas and priors, and stops with an error
if anything is inconsistent. It takes well under a second.

```{r prepare}
example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-annual-example.rds",
                               package = "multiScaleR"))
dat    <- example$data     # 100 counts from 25 sites over five years
inputs <- example$inputs   # prepared landscape inputs, distances in meters

response <- count ~ habitat + factor(year) + (1 | site)
scales   <- list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year))   # scale of effect varies by year
priors   <- list(scale_median = 250, scale_group_sd = 0.5)

prepared <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                             row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                             priors = priors, method = "prepare")
prepared
```

The printed object confirms the family, the number of observations, and the
scale formula. No sampling has happened yet.

# Run a short pilot

A short run tells you how long a full run will take and whether the sampler
moves freely. Slice sampling needs no extra software, so it is a convenient
first test.

```{r pilot-call, eval = FALSE}
pilot <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                          row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                          priors = priors,
                          method = "slice",   # sampler written in R
                          chains = 2,         # independent runs
                          iter = 1000,        # iterations per chain; half are warmup
                          seed = 5212)

pilot$diagnostics$passed                # did the sampler checks pass?
diagnose_bayes_scales(pilot)$parameters # checks on the quantities you report
```

```{r pilot-show, echo = FALSE}
pilot$diagnostics$passed
pilot$precision$parameters[c("quantity", "group", "rhat", "ess_bulk",
                             "ess_tail")]
```

**How to read the diagnostics:** The pilot took
`r round(pilot$seconds)` seconds and failed its checks, which is expected for
`r pilot$chain_dim[1]` retained iterations per chain. Three numbers matter.

- **`rhat`** compares the chains with one another. Values near 1 mean the
  chains agree. The package requires 1.01 or less.
- **`ess_bulk` and `ess_tail`** are effective sample sizes, or the number of
  independent draws the correlated chain is worth, for the center and the tails
  of the distribution. The package requires at least 100 per chain for each,
  which is `r 100 * pilot$chain_dim[2]` here.
- **`passed`** is `TRUE` only when every parameter meets both rules. NUTS fits
  must also have no divergences, no tree-depth hits, and an energy statistic
  (E-BFMI) of at least 0.3.

`fit$diagnostics` checks the raw model parameters. `diagnose_bayes_scales()`
adds the quantities you will report. Those are the log of each year's scale,
the spread of scales among years (`scale_group_sd`), and the spread of
baselines among sites (`response_group_sd`). Here the site spread is the
weakest, with a bulk effective sample size of
`r round(min(pilot$precision$parameters$ess_bulk))`.

# Extend the run or change the sampler

More iterations are the first remedy. The call below runs four chains of 8,000
iterations on four workers.

```{r long-call, eval = FALSE}
slice_long <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                               row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                               priors = priors, method = "slice",
                               chains = 4, iter = 8000, seed = 5213,
                               cores = 4)       # one chain per worker
```

The same model was also fitted with NUTS, and that fit is stored in the
example data.

```{r nuts-call, eval = FALSE}
nuts_fit <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                             row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                             priors = priors, method = "sample",
                             chains = 4, iter = 6000, warmup = 3000,
                             seed = 5211,
                             control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95,
                                            max_treedepth = 12))
```

```{r sampler-table, echo = FALSE}
nuts_fit  <- example$fits$pooled
nuts_info <- example$fit_info["pooled", ]
samplers <- data.frame(
  run = c("Slice pilot", "Slice, long", "NUTS"),
  draws = c(prod(pilot$chain_dim[1:2]), prod(long$chain_dim[1:2]),
            nuts_info$original_draws),
  seconds = c(pilot$seconds, long$seconds, nuts_info$seconds),
  rhat = c(max(pilot$diagnostics$parameters$rhat),
           max(long$diagnostics$parameters$rhat), nuts_info$max_rhat),
  ess = c(min(pilot$diagnostics$parameters$ess_bulk),
          min(long$diagnostics$parameters$ess_bulk), nuts_info$min_bulk_ess),
  passed = c(pilot$diagnostics$passed, long$diagnostics$passed,
             nuts_info$passed)
)
knitr::kable(samplers, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 3, 0, 0), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Run", "Retained draws", "Seconds", "Largest Rhat",
                           "Smallest bulk ESS", "Passed"))
```

**How to read the table:** Sixteen times as many draws brought the slice
sampler close, yet its largest Rhat is still
`r round(max(long$diagnostics$parameters$rhat), 3)` and its smallest effective
sample size is `r round(min(long$diagnostics$parameters$ess_bulk))`, short of
the `r 100 * long$chain_dim[2]` required. Site effects are the parameters that
lag. NUTS passed with fewer draws, because each of its draws is worth far
more. Its smallest effective sample size is
`r format(round(nuts_info$min_bulk_ess), big.mark = ",")` from
`r format(nuts_info$original_draws, big.mark = ",")` draws. The
slice run used four workers and the NUTS run used one, so the seconds are a
record of these runs and not a benchmark.

> **What this means for your study.** Compare samplers by effective sample
> size per second, not by iterations. A model with many site or year effects
> usually favors NUTS. Do not report a fit whose `passed` flag is `FALSE`,
> even when it fails narrowly.

# Use chains and cores

`chains` sets how many independent runs the sampler makes, and at least two
are needed for any diagnostic. `iter` is the length of each chain, and `warmup`
(half of `iter` by default) is the part discarded while the sampler tunes
itself. `cores` sets how many R processes work at once.

| Method | Work spread across cores |
|:-------|:-------------------------|
| `"sample"`, `"slice"` | Chains, so cores beyond the number of chains go unused |
| `"laplace"` | Optimizer starts (6 by default) |
| `"marginal"` | Optimizer starts at each grid point (3 by default) |
| `"marginal"` with importance correction | Optimizer starts, and evaluation of candidate draws |

Parallel work is not free. Each worker starts its own R process and holds its
own copy of the model. The two-chain pilot took `r round(pilot$seconds)`
seconds on one worker and `r round(cache$pilot_two_cores$seconds)` seconds on
two, and it returned identical draws both times because slice sampling uses the
same chain seeds at any core count. Save `cores` for runs that take minutes.

# Use an approximation when sampling is too slow

## Fit the approximations

```{r approximations, eval = FALSE}
# One Gaussian curve around the posterior peak
fast_fit <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                             row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                             priors = priors, method = "laplace",
                             laplace_draws = 2000, seed = 527001)

# Numerical integration over the spread of scales among years
marginal_fit <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                                 row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                                 priors = priors, method = "marginal",
                                 laplace_draws = 2000, seed = 527002)

# The same, reweighted against the full posterior
corrected_fit <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                                  row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                                  priors = priors, method = "marginal",
                                  laplace_draws = 2000, seed = 527003,
                                  control = list(correction = "importance",
                                                 importance_df = 5,
                                                 importance_min = 65536,
                                                 importance_max = 131072,
                                                 importance_refinements = 2))

fast_fit$diagnostics        # each fit stores its own numerical checks
```

`laplace_draws` sets how many draws are taken from the approximation for
summaries. More draws smooth the summaries and cannot repair a poor
approximation. `method = "marginal"` works only when the model has exactly one
spread of scales among groups, as `~1 + (1 | year)` does here. Each method has
its own checks, stored in `fit$diagnostics`.

| Method | `passed` requires |
|:-------|:------------------|
| `"laplace"` | The optimizer converged (`gradient_max` at most 0.0001), the curvature is valid (`min_eigenvalue` above 0, `condition_number` at most 1e12), and no second peak lies within 2 log-posterior units (`competing_modes`) |
| `"marginal"` | The same at every grid point, a finer grid leaves the answer unchanged (`grid_converged`), `competing_mass` at most 0.01, and `upper_tail_mass` at most 0.001 |
| Importance correction | `pareto_k` at most 0.7, `ess` at least 1,000, `min_tail_ess` at least 400, `max_weight` at most 0.01, and `split_cdf_error` at most 0.05 |

## Compare them with the samplers

The package stores the results of those three calls, alongside the NUTS fit.

```{r comparison}
comparison <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-computation-example.rds",
                                  package = "multiScaleR"))
print(comparison$availability, row.names = FALSE)   # status, run time, reason
```

In this table `nested` is the importance-corrected marginal fit. The next chunk
puts the spread of scales among years from every computation side by side.

```{r sd-table, echo = FALSE}
sd_rows <- subset(comparison$quantiles, type == "scale_sd")
sd_rows <- sd_rows[match(c("nuts", "laplace", "marginal", "nested"),
                         sd_rows$method), ]
slice_sd <- long$group_sd$log_scale_group_sd
sd_table <- data.frame(
  computation = c("NUTS", "Slice, long", "Laplace", "Marginal",
                  "Marginal, corrected"),
  checks = c("Passed", "Failed", "Passed", "Failed", "Passed"),
  seconds = c(nuts_info$seconds, long$seconds,
              comparison$availability$seconds),
  median = c(sd_rows$median[1], slice_sd$median, sd_rows$median[2:4]),
  lower  = c(sd_rows$lower[1],  slice_sd$lower,  sd_rows$lower[2:4]),
  upper  = c(sd_rows$upper[1],  slice_sd$upper,  sd_rows$upper[2:4])
)
knitr::kable(sd_table, digits = c(0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2), row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Computation", "Own checks", "Seconds",
                           "Spread among years", "Lower", "Upper"))
```

```{r annual-plot, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "***Scale of effect in each year from three computations of the same model. Points are posterior medians and bars are 95% intervals.***"}
annual <- subset(comparison$quantiles, type == "annual_log_scale" &
                   method != "marginal")
annual$year <- sub("year=", "", annual$label)
annual$computation <- factor(annual$method,
                             levels = c("nuts", "nested", "laplace"),
                             labels = c("NUTS", "Marginal, corrected",
                                        "Laplace"))
ggplot(annual, aes(x = year, y = exp(median), ymin = exp(lower),
                   ymax = exp(upper), color = computation)) +
  geom_pointrange(position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("black", "#2166AC", "#B2182B")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Scale of effect, sigma (m)", color = "Computation") +
  theme_classic()
```

**How to read the output:** The spread among years is on the log scale, so
exponentiate it. With a NUTS median of `r round(sd_table$median[1], 2)`, a year
one standard deviation above the typical year has a scale
`r round(exp(sd_table$median[1]), 2)` times the typical scale. Both the long
slice run and the corrected marginal fit agree with NUTS to within 0.01.
Laplace does not. It took `r round(sd_table$seconds[3], 1)` seconds and passed
all of its own checks, yet its median of `r round(sd_table$median[3], 2)` is
more than twice the NUTS value. Its yearly scales in the figure are shifted
upward as well, to a median of
`r round(exp(annual$median[annual$method == "laplace"][1]))` m in 2021 against
`r round(exp(annual$median[annual$method == "nuts"][1]))` m. Because the
uncorrected marginal fit failed its grid check, do not use its median of
`r round(sd_table$median[4], 2)`.

The gap is not peculiar to this example. In simulations of three other
designs, the probability that a year's scale fell below a set distance
differed from NUTS by more than 0.05, well beyond Monte Carlo error, in 49 of
87 comparisons for Laplace fits and 39 of 71 for uncorrected marginal fits.

> **What this means for your study.** A passed check on an approximation says
> the arithmetic finished cleanly. It does not say the approximation is close
> to the posterior. Before you report an approximate fit, compare it once with
> a sampler on the same model or on a subset of the data.

The corrected marginal fit matched NUTS here and took longer
(`r round(sd_table$seconds[5])` against `r round(sd_table$seconds[1])`
seconds), so it offered no advantage for this model. Summarize a corrected fit
with `posterior_scales(corrected_fit, estimator = "weighted")`, which uses the
importance weights directly.

The correction also tracked NUTS in simulations of eight designs with
Gaussian, Poisson, binomial, or negative binomial responses. Across 5,282
scale probabilities, the largest difference from NUTS was 0.033. Matching NUTS
is not the same as a calibrated interval. In one repeated-site Poisson design,
90% intervals for the first year's scale held the true value in 39 of 48 data
sets for the corrected fits and 38 of 48 for NUTS. The evidence covers those
designs only.

## Check one probability from an uncorrected approximation

When sampling is out of reach, `diagnose_bayes_laplace()` checks one kind of
number from a Laplace or uncorrected marginal fit. That number is the
probability that a year's scale is at or below a distance you name. The
function draws a fresh, deliberately wide sample around the approximation,
reweights every draw against the full posterior, and compares the reweighted
probability with the one the approximation gave. The function is
experimental and needs the RTMB and posterior packages.

```{r laplace-check, eval = FALSE}
# Probability that each year's scale is 150 m or less, and 350 m or less
check <- diagnose_bayes_laplace(fast_fit,
                                thresholds = list(habitat = c(150, 350)),
                                tolerance  = 0.05,     # difference that matters
                                candidates = 65536,    # size of the fresh sample
                                seed       = 127)
check$probabilities[, c("group", "threshold", "approximation", "reference",
                        "status")]
```

Each row of `check$probabilities` is one year and one threshold. Read the
`status` column.

| `status` | Meaning | What to do |
|:---------|:--------|:-----------|
| `"discrepancy"` | The approximation and the reweighted reference differ by more than `tolerance`, beyond Monte Carlo error | Do not report the approximate probability. Sample the model |
| `"within_tolerance"` | They agree within `tolerance` for this year and threshold | The approximate probability can be reported, for this threshold only |
| `"unresolved"` | The reference is too imprecise, or overlaps the posterior too poorly, to decide | Treat the probability as unchecked. Raise `candidates`, or sample |

In 35 simulated data sets, the check flagged 54 of 135 real differences for
Laplace fits and 21 of 67 for marginal fits, and it never marked a real
difference as within tolerance. Most checks, 448 of 630, were unresolved,
including every one in models with repeated site effects. Expect
`"unresolved"` often, and read it as "not checked", not as "close enough".

# Check the precision of the numbers you report

A credible interval describes what the data leave uncertain. *Monte Carlo
error* describes how precisely a finite number of draws pins down that
interval. `diagnose_bayes_scales()` reports it as `mcse`, the Monte Carlo
standard error of each quantile.

```{r precision-call, eval = FALSE}
precision <- diagnose_bayes_scales(slice_long)
precision$quantiles     # median and interval limits, each with its mcse
```

```{r precision-show, echo = FALSE}
q <- subset(long$precision$quantiles, group == "year=2021")
q[c("quantity", "group", "probability", "estimate", "mcse")]
```

**How to read the output:** Estimates for a scale are natural logs of meters.
For 2021 the lower limit is `r round(q$estimate[1], 2)`, or
`r round(exp(q$estimate[1]))` m, with an `mcse` of `r round(q$mcse[1], 3)`. An
error of that size on the log scale is about `r round(100 * q$mcse[1])`% of the
distance, so repeating the run would move this limit by a meter or two. Compare
that with the credible interval itself, which spans
`r round(exp(q$estimate[1]))` to `r round(exp(q$estimate[3]))` m. The
computation is far more precise than the data are informative.

For a specific threshold, `diagnose_bayes_probabilities()` reports the
posterior probability that a scale is at or below it.

```{r probability-call, eval = FALSE}
diagnose_bayes_probabilities(slice_long,
                             thresholds = list(habitat = c(100, 250)),  # meters
                             mcse_target = 0.005)$probabilities
```

```{r probability-show, echo = FALSE}
p <- subset(cache$probabilities$probabilities, group == "year=2021")
p[c("group", "threshold", "estimate", "mcse", "precision_target_met")]
```

**In a report.** "The posterior probability that the 2021 scale of
effect was 250 m or less was `r round(p$estimate[2], 2)` (Monte Carlo standard
error `r round(p$mcse[2], 3)`)." The run missed the requested precision of
0.005, so report two decimal places and no more.

Both functions need the original chains. The stored example fits keep only
2,000 thinned draws, so they return `available = FALSE` with the reason.

# Plan for run time and memory

- **Time a pilot and scale up from it.** The pilot here ran about
  `r round(pilot$sampling$chains * pilot$sampling$iter / pilot$seconds)`
  iterations per second. At that rate, four chains of 8,000 iterations need
  about `r round(4 * 8000 / (pilot$sampling$chains * pilot$sampling$iter / pilot$seconds) / 60)`
  minutes on one worker.
- **A fitted object keeps its chains.** The long slice fit held
  `r long$chain_dim[1]` iterations of `r long$chain_dim[3]` parameters in each
  of `r long$chain_dim[2]` chains and occupied
  `r round(long$fit_bytes / 1e6)` MB.
- **Prediction can need more than fitting.** `predict()` computes one value
  per posterior draw and observation, at 8 bytes each. With 2,000 draws, a map
  of 100,000 cells needs 1.6 GB. Lower `draws`, or predict in blocks when you
  need only a summary for each location.
- **Each worker holds a copy of the model.** Memory use rises with `cores`.

# What to do when a fit struggles

| What you see | What to try |
|:-------------|:------------|
| `diagnostics$passed` is `FALSE` with a large `rhat` or small effective sample size | Raise `iter`. If a slice fit still fails, switch to `method = "sample"` |
| A NUTS fit reports divergences or tree-depth hits | Raise `adapt_delta` (default 0.9) or `max_treedepth` (default 12) in `control`. The stored fits used `adapt_delta` of 0.95 and 0.99 |
| A Laplace fit stops with an error or warns of competing modes | Add starts with `control = list(starts = 10, iter.max = 1500)`, or sample |
| A marginal fit has `grid_converged = FALSE` | Refine the grid with `control = list(max_grid = 257)`, or sample |
| A corrected fit fails its weight checks | Raise `importance_min` and `importance_max`, set `importance_df = 5` for heavier tails, or sample |
| `diagnose_bayes_laplace()` reports `"discrepancy"` or `"unresolved"` for a probability you need | Sample the model before you report that probability |
| `method = "marginal"` stops because the model has more than one spread of scales among groups | Use `"sample"`, `"slice"`, or `"laplace"` |
| Every check passes, but much of a scale's posterior lies below `min_D` or above `max_D` | The data say little about that scale. Review the priors and `max_D` in `vignette("v13-bayesian-scales", package = "multiScaleR")` |

Keep the model, priors, and data fixed while you compare computations. If a
check fails, change the computation and leave the thresholds alone.

# Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval = FALSE}
# 1. Check the software and the model
check_bayes_setup("sample")
prepared <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                             row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                             priors = priors, method = "prepare")

# 2. Short pilot: time it and read the diagnostics
pilot <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                          row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                          priors = priors, method = "slice",
                          chains = 2, iter = 1000, seed = 5212)
pilot$diagnostics$passed                  # FALSE: extend or change sampler
diagnose_bayes_scales(pilot)$parameters   # Rhat and ESS for reported quantities

# 3. Full run with NUTS
nuts_fit <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                             row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                             priors = priors, method = "sample",
                             chains = 4, iter = 6000, warmup = 3000,
                             seed = 5211,
                             control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95,
                                            max_treedepth = 12))
summary(nuts_fit)$diagnostics             # passed, divergences, Rhat, ESS

# 4. Precision of what you report (needs the original chains)
diagnose_bayes_scales(nuts_fit)$quantiles # interval limits with their mcse
diagnose_bayes_probabilities(nuts_fit,
                             thresholds = list(habitat = c(100, 250)),
                             mcse_target = 0.005)$probabilities

# 5. A fast approximation. Compare it with a sampler before you report it
fast_fit <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, scales = scales,
                             row_id = "site_year", family = "nbinom2",
                             priors = priors, method = "laplace",
                             laplace_draws = 2000, seed = 527001)
fast_fit$diagnostics                      # numerical checks only
diagnose_bayes_laplace(fast_fit, thresholds = list(habitat = c(150, 350)),
                       candidates = 65536, seed = 127)$probabilities
                                          # "unresolved" means not checked
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|:---------|:--------|
| `check_bayes_setup()` | Report whether the optional packages for a method are installed |
| `multiScale_bayes()` | Fit the model. `method` chooses the computation |
| `summary()` | Report estimates and the stored diagnostics of a fit |
| `diagnose_bayes_scales()` | Check chain agreement and Monte Carlo error for the scales and spreads you report |
| `diagnose_bayes_probabilities()` | Report the probability that a scale is at or below a threshold, with its Monte Carlo error |
| `diagnose_bayes_laplace()` | Check such a probability from an uncorrected approximation against a reweighted reference |
| `posterior_scales()` | Summarize scales in map units. `estimator = "weighted"` uses importance weights |
